intros.market: Five CAs control 88% of publicly trusted certificate issuance, led by Internet Security Research Group at 32% and Google Trust Services at 21%. The CR3 ratio stands at 71%, indicating high concentration in a market of 88 trusted CAs. DigiCert, GoDaddy, and Sectigo complete the top five, while 74 CAs collectively hold the remaining 12% of market share.
intros.trust: The four major root stores contain 335 total roots representing 88 distinct CA owners, but only 38 owners appear in all four stores and just 90 roots are universally trusted. Microsoft maintains 142 roots not present in Chrome, Mozilla, or Apple, creating operational complexity where certificate chains trusted in Edge may fail validation in other browsers. This fragmentation means CAs must navigate four different trust boundaries with minimal overlap, and the variance in store policies compounds the concentration seen in issuance share.
intros.conc: The WebPKI exhibits moderate concentration with an HHI of 1,984, well above the 1,500 threshold that triggers antitrust scrutiny in traditional markets. Two CAs alone command 53% of issuance, creating systemic dependency where operational failures at Internet Security Research Group or Google Trust Services would immediately affect a majority of the web. This concentration intersects with the 88-CA trust surface to create a bifurcated ecosystem where a handful of operators shoulder most production risk.
intros.tail: Seventy-four CAs in the long tail collectively issue just 12% of certificates yet retain full trust store inclusion and the capability to issue for any domain. These low-volume operators face the same compliance obligations as high-volume leaders but lack the economies of scale, engineering resources, and incident detection capabilities that larger CAs deploy. The tail contributes disproportionately to operational risk, as limited issuance provides minimal statistical signal for anomaly detection while full trust conveys maximum impact from compromise or misissuance.
intros.geo: CAs incorporated in the United States issue 92.81% of all publicly trusted certificates, despite representing only 15 of 84 trusted CA organizations. European CAs account for 7.1% of issuance across 44 organizations, while 17 Asia-Pacific CAs collectively issue 0.09% of certificates. This extreme geographic concentration creates single-jurisdiction exposure where changes to US law, regulatory posture, or legal process immediately affect nine in ten certificates securing web traffic globally.
intros.gov: Thirty state-operated or state-owned CAs hold positions in public root stores, representing more than one-third of all trusted CA organizations. These government-controlled entities collectively issue 0.09% of certificates, roughly matching the entire Asia-Pacific commercial sector in volume. Their trust store presence grants technical capability to issue for any domain regardless of actual issuance patterns, creating a gap between observed behavior and potential state surveillance or interception scenarios.
intros.jurisdiction: Five jurisdictions carry high legal risk due to compelled disclosure laws, surveillance frameworks, or state access requirements: China, Russia, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Hong Kong. India and Turkey present moderate risk with evolving data localization and government access mandates. These classifications intersect with both the 30 government-operated CAs and the geographic concentration in the United States, where CAs face legal process under FISA Section 702, national security letters, and sealed court orders that may compel cooperation without public disclosure.
intros.ops: CAs have disclosed 1,705 incidents across 55 organizations, led by 656 misissuance events and 552 governance failures. Only 30% of incidents are self-detected, while 18% are discovered by external researchers and 15% by automated tools, indicating systemic surveillance gaps in CA operations. Root program oversight covers just 18.4% of incidents in Chrome and 9.9% in Mozilla as of 2025, down from 67.8% and 78.0% respectively in 2019, suggesting deteriorating governance effectiveness as incident volume grows.
intros.crypto: Root certificate algorithms, key sizes, and cryptographic agility determine the technical foundation for trust decisions and upgrade pathways. Modern roots predominantly use RSA 4096-bit or ECDSA P-384 keys with SHA-256 signatures, meeting current NIST and CA/Browser Forum requirements. Legacy roots with RSA 2048-bit keys or SHA-1 signatures remain in some trust stores, creating compatibility versus security tradeoffs that mirror the cross-store disagreement patterns in trust surface data.
intros.distrust: Browsers have executed 16 distrust events against CAs, with 14 attributed to compliance or operational failures rather than compromise. Seven cases involved negligent noncompliance, three demonstrated incompetence, and three constituted willful circumvention of requirements. The median runway from distrust announcement to enforcement is 1,185 days, providing substantial migration time but also extending the window where known-deficient CAs continue issuing trusted certificates.
intros.policy: Active TLS-issuing CAs show a median certificate validity period of 62 days against SC-081 requirements of 200 days by March 2026, 100 days by March 2027, and 47 days by March 2029, with eight CAs already at or below the 47-day target and five still above 100 days. This operational readiness challenge unfolds against a compliance surface that has grown 121-fold since 2000 to 6,657 total obligations across CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements, four root program policies, WebTrust and ETSI audit criteria, and IETF/NIST standards. Seventy-six percent of these obligations are mandatory, yet no new ballots have passed since 2022 even as CAs navigate validity reduction timelines, suggesting the ecosystem struggles to adapt policy as operational complexity compounds.
intros.governance: Chrome provided substantive oversight on 18.4% of the 223 disclosed incidents in 2025, down from 67.8% coverage in 2019, while Mozilla fell from 78.0% to 9.9% over the same period. Apple commented substantively on 5.4% of incidents and Microsoft on none, despite all four programs theoretically enforcing overlapping baseline requirements. This deteriorating coverage occurs as the bug corpus reaches 1,997 total cases and incident volume remains above 200 annually, indicating that root program resources have not scaled with ecosystem growth or that programs have deprioritized public oversight in favor of private enforcement.
intros.community: The CA/Browser Forum has 56 member organizations but only 21 contribute actively to standards development, while 35 have made zero ballot contributions. Stephen Davidson of Sectigo leads individual participation with 36 ballots proposed, and Sectigo itself ranks as the most active organization. This concentration of policy work among a small subset of members means that many CAs bound by Forum requirements have no voice in their formation, and the silent majority of 35 members suggests widespread free-riding on governance labor.
intros.audit: Independent audits detected just 28% of incidents that occurred during their in-period scope, with 118 incidents caught out of 429 that auditors should have covered in their letters. Forty-two CAs show high transparency gaps between clean audit opinions and disclosed incident histories, while six auditors issued qualified opinions noting control deficiencies. WebTrust self-reporting stands at 62.4% and ETSI at 69.4%, indicating that roughly one-third of required audit updates are missing or late, and only 12 CAs have adopted the newer ETSI EN 319 411-1 v3.5 standard despite six auditor changes in 2025 signaling market dissatisfaction with audit quality.
